d: One praying humbly for something
ety: From French suppliant, present participle of supplier. Doublet of supplicant.
s: I touch your beard as a suppliant, embrace your knees, imploring you to have pity on my wretchedness.

d: Devoid of intelligence
ety: From Latin fatuus (“foolish, silly, simple”).
s: Maude Lebowski: Lord. You can imagine where it goes from here. The Dude: He fixes the cable? Maude: Don't be fatuous, Jeffrey.

d: An engine that provided medieval artillery used during sieges; a heavy war engine for hurling large stones and other missiles
ety: From Middle English onager, onagir (“wild ass; military catapult”), from Anglo-Norman onager, Middle French onager, onagre, Old French onager, onagre (“wild ass; military catapult”) (modern French onagre), from Late Latin onager (“large siege engine”), Latin onager (“wild ass”), from Hellenistic Ancient Greek ὄναγρος (ónagros, “wild ass”), Byzantine Ancient Greek ὄναγρος (ónagros, “large siege eng
s: One of the onagers, however, having hurt its leg, could not be harnessed at present, and a few days' rest was necessary.

d: Large heavy rope for nautical use
ety: From Middle English hauser, haucer, from Anglo-Norman haucer, from Vulgar Latin *altiāre (“to raise”), derived from Latin altus (“high”). Altered in English by mistaken association with hawse and perhaps haul. Compare French aussière, haussière.
s: A hatchet to my hawser? all adrift to go?

d: Power to influence or coerce
ety: From Middle English puissaunce, from Anglo-Norman puissance, pusaunce, and other forms, from Old French puissant (“powerful”).
s: We easily pronounce puissance, truth and justice; they be words importing some great matter, but that thing we neither see nor conceive.

d: Overbearing pride evidenced by a superior manner toward inferiors
ety: Borrowed from French hauteur.
s: Sometimes the hauteur is nothing more dire than a kind of black-mother wit.

d: An officer of the church who is in charge of sacred objects
ety: From French sacristain, Late Latin sacrista, from Latin sacer. Doublet of sexton.
s: The church was looked after by an old sacristan who lived in a cottage on the shore of the lake.

d: The belief in magical spells that harness occult forces or evil spirits to produce unnatural effects in the world
ety: Circa 1300, from Middle English nigromancye, from Old French nigromancie, from Medieval Latin nigromantia, from Latin necromantia, from Ancient Greek νεκρομαντεία (nekromanteía), νεκρός (nekrós, “dead”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”). Medieval Latin spelling, incorporating niger (“black”), influenced by the notion of black art. Modern spelling adopted in mid-1500s. By surface analysis, necro- +
s: There is no doubt..that necromancy is the touch-stone of occultism...

d: Excluded from use or mention
ety: Unadapted borrowing from German verboten (“banned, forbidden, prohibited”). Doublet of forbidden.
s: Before that, students and professors could date whomever we wanted; the next day we were off-limits to one another—verboten, traife, dangerous (and perhaps, therefore, all the more alluring).

d: Temporary cessation or suspension
ety: First attested in 1528. From Anglo-Norman abeiance (“legal expectation”), from Old French abeance (“desire”) from abeër (“to gape at, aspire after”), abaer, abair (“to desire”), from a (“to”) + baër (“to gape”), bair (“yawn”), from Medieval Latin batō (“to yawn”).
s: Without a plausible explanation for what might have provoked an ice age, the whole theory fell into abeyance.

d: Not easily perturbed or excited or upset; marked by extreme calm and composure
s: Hitherto imperturbable, he now showed signs of alarm.

d: A spinning machine formerly used to twist and wind fibers of cotton or wool continuously
ety: From Middle English throstle, throstel, from Old English þrostle, from Proto-West Germanic *þrostlā, possibly altered from or a diminutive of *þurstaz, related to *þrastuz, from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos.
s: O Lady! in this wan and heartless mood / To other thoughts by yonder throstle woo'd

d: A strong north wind that blows in France during the winter
ety: Borrowed from Middle French mistral, from Occitan. Doublet of magistral.
s: The mistral had been blowing for three days now and the sea showed more white than blue

d: The slender spear of the Bantu-speaking people of Africa
ety: From French azagaie (now zagaie) or Portuguese azagaia, Spanish azagaya, and later in the forms that have become most common borrowed from Afrikaans assegaai, from colloquial Arabic اَلزَّغَايَة (az-zaḡāya), from Proto-Berber *zaġāya (“spear”).
s: Native mats covered the clay walls; a collection of spears, assegais, shields, knives was hung up in trophies.

d: Prevent the occurrence of; prevent from happening
ety: From Middle English forfenden (“to ward off, protect, prohibit”), equivalent to for- + fend.
s: People have long given thought to the causes of danger and how they might be forfended.

d: A ceramic or mural decoration made by scratching off a surface layer to reveal the ground
ety: Borrowed from Italian sgraffito, from s- (“out”) + graffito (past participle of graffire), ultimately from Ancient Greek γράφειν (gráphein, “to write or scratch”).
s: I did murals there as well, designs for windows, bas relief and otherwise, sgraffitoes – a very special technique cut in stucco.

d: A hussar’s jacket worn over the shoulders
ety: Apparently from French doliman, dolman (sense 2), ultimately from Ottoman Turkish طولامان, دولامان (dolaman, “robe”), from طولامق (dolamak, “to wrap around”). Compare German Doliman, Dollman; Hungarian dolmány.
s: Sitting on the chair's edge, he shrugged a shoulder until his dolman fell into place, then balanced his helmet on his knee like a pampered pet.

d: Impossible to avoid or evade
ety: From Middle French inéluctable (whence in- + e- and -able), from Latin inēlūctābilis, from in- + ēlūctor (“struggle out”) + -bilis.
s: They have come under the yoke of ineluctable slavery.

d: Arousing or provoking laughter
ety: From Middle French risible and directly from Late Latin rīsibilis, from Latin rīsus (“laughter”) + -ibilis, from the perfect passive participle of rīdeō (“laugh”).
s: Do you find it risible when I say the name, 'Biggus Dickus'?

d: Talk socially without exchanging too much information
ety: From a Northern England dialectal variant of gnatter (also knatter) ("to chatter, grumble; nibble away at"), ultimately of imitative origin. Cognate with German Low German gnattern (“to mumble, grumble, be grouchy”).
s: What are you guys nattering about? You're clearly not following the meeting!

d: A person who drinks alcohol to excess habitually
ety: From dipso- + -maniac.
s: The dipsomaniac and the abstainer are not only both mistaken, but they both make the same mistake. They both regard wine as a drug and not as a drink.

d: Requiring secret or mysterious knowledge
ety: Borrowed from Latin arcānus (“hidden, secret”), from arceō (“to shut up, enclose”); cognate with Latin arca (“a chest”).
s: He had an arcane knowledge of ancient rituals.

d: Tending to promote physical well-being; beneficial to health
ety: Borrowed from Middle French salutaire and its source, Latin salutaris (“healthful”), from salus (“health”).
s: Using such neofuturists as Nicholas Negroponte to support his argument, Groper argues that “being digital” is constitutive of today’s salutary political life (167).

d: Thick cushion used as a seat
ety: From Old English hassoc (“coarse grass”), of uncertain origin.
s: At the next service he found a flower on his hassock and a highly suggestive Catholic bookmarker tucked into his hymn-book.

d: Dull and tiresome but with pretensions of significance or originality
ety: From platitude + -ous on analogy of other adjectives ending in -tudinous, from Latin -tūdin- + -ous, the oblique stem of -tūdō. Compare platitudinize.
s: Viewed simply as a novel, “Lolita” deals with situations and emotions that would remain exasperatingly vague to the reader had their expression been etiolated by means of platitudinous evasions.

d: A crafty and involved plot to achieve your (usually sinister) ends
ety: From Middle English machynacion, machynacyon, from Middle French machination and directly Latin māchinātiōnem, from māchinor (“devise, invent”). By surface analysis, machinate + -ion or machine + -ation.
s: PATRICK: The inner machinations of my mind are an enigma.

d: Total certainty or greater certainty than circumstances warrant
ety: From Middle French certitude, from Late Latin certitūdō, from Latin certus.
s: Taxes are obviously certitudes.

d: Offer as a sacrifice by killing or by giving up to destruction
ety: The adjective is first attested in 1534, the verb in 1548; borrowed from Latin immolātus, perfect passive participle of immolō (“to sacrifice”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
s: The Aztecs immolated human victims.

d: Dedicated in fulfillment of a vow
ety: From Middle French votif, from Latin vōtīvus (“votive”), from vōtum (“vow”).
s: She placed a votive offering at the shrine.

d: Ostentatiously lofty in style
ety: Equivalent to declaim + -atory.
s: Behind him an excitable Frenchman was holding forth in declamatory style to a group of astonished residents.

d: A relatively small amount of money given for services rendered (as by a waiter)
ety: From Turkish bahşiş, from Persian بخشیش (baxšiš, “present; an honorary or pecuniary gratuity; drink-money”) or بخشش (baxšeš), from بخشیدن (baxšidan, “to give, grant, bestow”).
s: Baksheesh (lubrication payment) is often the accepted manner of doing business in the Middle and Far East. However, one must be careful not to confuse ethics with the law.

d: A concise reference book providing specific information about a subject or location
ety: Either via Latin enchīridion or directly, from Ancient Greek ἐγχειρίδιον (enkheirídion, “handbook, manual”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + -ίδιον (-ídion).
s: Sartor Resartus was for many years his Enchiridion (he says), while the translations from the German, the references to German literature and philosophy, fired him to read the originals.

d: In good time
ety: From Middle English betymes, from bi (“by”) + time + adverbial -s. By surface analysis, betime + -s (adverbial suffix). Compare also betides.
s: Smart lad to slip betimes away From fields where glory does not stay.

d: Rip off; ask an unreasonable price
ety: Possibly from Yiddish גזלן (gazlen, “thief, bandit”).
s: The tactic was to gazump the Labour Party and the FOL by a major restructuring of the tax system.

d: Traffic in ecclesiastical offices or preferments
ety: From Middle English simonie, symonye, from Old French simonie, from Late Latin simonia, named after Simon Magus (Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (Šimʻôn, “Simon”)), with reference to Acts 8:18–20.
s: He openly practiced simony; in other words, he sold benefices.

d: A sleeveless cape that is lined or trimmed with fur
ety: Borrowed from French pelisse, from Late Latin pellicia, from Latin pellis (“skin”). Doublet of pilch.
s: The mother was crimson in countenance and pelisse, and her ample dimensions spoke years of peace and plenteousness.

d: Add details, as to an account or idea; clarify the meaning of and discourse in a learned way, usually in writing
ety: From the participle stem of Latin expatior, from ex- + spatior (“walk about”).
s: “It can't fly,” he expatiated. “It can move forward only by hopping.”

d: Written in the form of or carried on by letters or correspondence
ety: 1627, from Latin epistolārius, from epistola (“letter”) (English epistle) + -ārius, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ) from ἐπιστέλλω (epistéllō, “to send a message”) from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to prepare, send”). For the noun, compare Middle English pistelarie and Old English pistelari, both from Medieval Latin epistolārium, possibly via an unattested *epistelari, *epistolarie.
s: Bram Stoker's novel Dracula (1897) is written in epistolary style.

d: Containing or implying a slight or showing prejudice
ety: Borrowed from Latin invidiōsus, from invidia (“envy, ill will”), from in- (“upon”) + videō (“to see”); the meaning developed from “look back at” to “look askance at” to “envy.” Doublet of envious, from Old French.
s: But the rich man—not to make any invidious comparison—is always sold to the institution which makes him rich.

d: A flowery and highly rhetorical oration
ety: From Latin perōrō (“to speak at length, to conclude a speech”) (from per- (“very”) + ōrō (“to speak, to orate”) (English orate)) + -ation (“action (nominalizer)”) (from Latin -ātiō).
s: Nephew, what means this passionate discourse, This peroration with such circumstance?
